title: Ecosystems and Food Webs
seo_title: Grade 6 Natural Sciences and Technology: Ecosystems and Food Webs Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_code: Grade 6 Natural Sciences and Technology: Ecosystems and food webs
standard_text: An ecosystem is made up of plants, animals and the non-living environment interacting in one place. Food webs show how many food chains link together. Decomposers break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil. (summary of CAPS Natural Sciences and Technology, Grade 6, Life and Living: Ecosystems and food webs)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 Natural Sciences and Technology worksheets (CAPS): ecosystems, food chains and food webs, producers, consumers and decomposers, and changes in a food web. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A food web is many food chains linked together.
body_html:
How to think about it

An ecosystem is all the living things in an area (plants, animals, fungi and micro-organisms) together with the non-living things (water, soil, air, sunlight). Examples are a grassland, a wetland and a rock pool.

Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so food chains link into a food web. Producers make food, consumers eat food, and decomposers (fungi, bacteria, earthworms) break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil.

Example

What do decomposers do?

Think of a fallen tree.

Answer: break down dead material and return nutrients

Example

Why is a food web more realistic than one food chain?

How many foods does an animal eat?

Answer: animals eat more than one kind of food

Common mistakes

  • Thinking decomposers are pests.
  • Thinking a food web has only one producer.
  • Forgetting the non-living part of an ecosystem.

faq.q: What happens to a food web if the producers die?
faq.a: All the consumers lose their source of energy.

faq.q: Is the Sun part of an ecosystem?
faq.a: It is a non-living factor that provides the energy for the ecosystem.

items.q: Is a mushroom a plant?
c: No. It is a fungus, a decomposer that cannot make its own food.
No, it is an animal that hunts.
items.e: Fungi get food from dead matter.

items.q: A saltbush dies in a drought. What happens to the matter in it over time?
c: Decomposers break it down and return nutrients to the soil.
items.e: Fungi, bacteria and small animals recycle dead matter.

items.q: Which of these is a producer?
items.e: Algae is a producer.

items.q: A zebra dies in a paddock. What happens to the matter in it over time?
c: Decomposers break it down and return nutrients to the soil.
items.e: Fungi, bacteria and small animals recycle dead matter.

items.q: Is banksia a producer, a consumer or a decomposer?
items.e: Producers make their own food from sunlight.

items.q: A lion dies in the bush. What happens to the matter in it over time?
c: Decomposers break it down and return nutrients to the soil.
items.e: Fungi, bacteria and small animals recycle dead matter.

items.q: Which of these is a consumer?
items.e: Dugong is a consumer.

items.q: A compost bin turns food scraps into soil. Which living things do this?
c: decomposers such as worms, fungi and bacteria
items.e: Composting uses decomposers.

items.q: What would happen if there were no decomposers?
c: Dead plants and animals would pile up and soil would lose nutrients.
items.e: Decomposers recycle nutrients.

items.q: Is a blue gum tree a producer, a consumer or a decomposer?
items.e: Producers make their own food from sunlight.

items.q: Is a zebra a producer, a consumer or a decomposer?
items.e: Consumers get energy by eating other living things.

items.q: Seagrass grows in shallow sea water. What is its role?
c: a producer that feeds dugongs and turtles
items.e: Seagrass makes food from sunlight.

items.q: Leaves fall from a wattle onto the ground. What happens to the matter in it over time?
c: Decomposers break it down and return nutrients to the soil.
items.e: Fungi, bacteria and small animals recycle dead matter.

items.q: A blue gum tree falls over in a storm. What happens to the matter in it over time?
c: Decomposers break it down and return nutrients to the soil.
items.e: Fungi, bacteria and small animals recycle dead matter.

items.q: Is a wild dog a producer, a consumer or a decomposer?
items.e: Consumers get energy by eating other living things.

items.q: Is a dugong a producer, a consumer or a decomposer?
items.e: Consumers get energy by eating other living things.

items.q: What does a producer need to make its food?
c: sunlight, water and carbon dioxide from the air
items.e: Plants make food in their leaves.

items.q: What happens to a fallen blue gum tree in a forest over many years?
c: Fungi, bacteria and insects break it down into soil.
items.e: Decomposers recycle the matter.

items.q: Is saltbush a producer, a consumer or a decomposer?
items.e: Producers make their own food from sunlight.

items.q: Which of these is a decomposer?
items.e: Mushroom is a decomposer.

items.q: In the food chain leaves → caterpillar → magpie, which animal is the top predator?
items.e: The top predator is at the end of the chain; nothing in the chain eats it.

items.q: In a food chain, what does the arrow in “mouse → brown snake” mean?
c: The mouse eats the brown snake.
The mouse lives far from the brown snake.
The brown snake eats the mouse.
The mouse and the brown snake are the same size.
items.e: Arrows point from the food to the eater: they show which way energy flows.

items.q: What is a herbivore?
c: an animal that eats only animals
an animal that eats only plants
items.e: Lions and zebras are herbivores.

items.q: In the food chain native grass → ant → thorny devil, which animal is the top predator?
items.e: The top predator is at the end of the chain; nothing in the chain eats it.

items.q: In the food chain seaweed → green turtle, which living thing is the producer?
items.e: The producer makes its own food from sunlight and comes first.

items.q: Where does the energy in every food chain first come from?
items.e: Producers use sunlight to make food.

items.q: In the chain grass → zebra → wild dog, which is the prey of the wild dog?
items.e: Prey is the animal eaten.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Which animal eats the parrotfish?
items.e: Follow the arrow away from the parrotfish.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Which food chain is part of this food web?
c: phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → coral trout → reef shark
zooplankton → phytoplankton → small fish → coral trout → reef shark
reef shark → coral trout → small fish → zooplankton → phytoplankton
phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → coral trout → seaweed
items.e: Each arrow points from the food to the animal that eats it.

items.q: In the food chain grass → zebra → wild dog, which animal is the top predator?
items.e: The top predator is at the end of the chain; nothing in the chain eats it.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Which organism is a producer?
items.e: Producers are plants that make their own food using light.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Which animal eats the zooplankton?
items.e: Follow the arrow away from the zooplankton.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Which of these does the parrotfish eat?
items.e: The arrow points from the food to the parrotfish.

items.q: In a food chain, what does the arrow in “yabby → Murray cod” mean?
c: The yabby eats the Murray cod.
The Murray cod eats the yabby.
The yabby and the Murray cod are the same size.
The yabby lives far from the Murray cod.
items.e: Arrows point from the food to the eater: they show which way energy flows.

items.q: Which living thing is always at the start of a food chain?
c: a producer, such as a plant
items.e: Producers make their own food.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Which animal eats the small fish?
items.e: Follow the arrow away from the small fish.

items.q: In a food chain, what does the arrow in “seaweed → green turtle” mean?
c: The seaweed lives far from the green turtle.
The green turtle eats the seaweed.
The seaweed and the green turtle are the same size.
The seaweed eats the green turtle.
items.e: Arrows point from the food to the eater: they show which way energy flows.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Which of these does the green turtle eat?
items.e: The arrow points from the food to the green turtle.

items.q: What is a predator?
c: an animal that hunts and eats other animals
items.e: The animal that is eaten is the prey.

items.q: What is a carnivore?
c: an animal that eats only other animals
an animal that eats only plants
items.e: Wild dogs and reef sharks are carnivores.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Most of the small fish are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the small fish eats zooplankton in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. A disease kills most of the zooplankton. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The small fish eats only zooplankton in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. In this web, the parrotfish eats seaweed. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores only animals, omnivores both.

items.q: Look at the coral reef food web. In this web, the zooplankton's food is: phytoplankton. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: It eats only plants (producers).

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. A disease kills most of the small fish. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The coral trout eats only a small fish in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Which organism is not eaten by any other organism in this web?
items.e: No arrow leaves the green turtle.

items.q: Use the coral reef food web. Which animal eats the zooplankton?
items.e: An arrow goes from the zooplankton to the small fish.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Which organism is not eaten by any other organism in this web?
items.e: No arrow leaves the reef shark.

items.q: This is a pond food web. How many kinds of food does the turtle eat in this web?
items.e: Count the arrows pointing to the turtle: snail, pondweed.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. In this web, the green turtle eats seaweed. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores only animals, omnivores both.

items.q: Use the forest food web. How many kinds of food does the wolf eat in this web?
items.e: Count the arrows pointing to the wolf: deer.

items.q: This is a coral reef food web. Which animal eats the seaweed?
items.e: An arrow goes from the seaweed to the parrotfish.

items.q: This is a coral reef food web. How many kinds of food does the parrotfish eat in this web?
items.e: Count the arrows pointing to the parrotfish: seaweed.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. A disease kills most of the seaweed. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The parrotfish eats only seaweed in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. A disease kills most of the phytoplankton. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The zooplankton eats only phytoplankton in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: This is an ocean food web. In this web, the orca's food is: seal, sea otter. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: It eats only animals.

items.q: Use the meadow food web. What does the frog eat?
items.e: The arrow goes from the grasshopper to the frog, so the frog eats a grasshopper.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. In this web, the coral trout eats small fish. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores only animals, omnivores both.

items.q: Use the pond food web. Which of these is food for the snail?
items.e: The arrow goes from the algae to the snail, so the snail eats algae.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Most of the coral trout are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the coral trout eats small fish in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Few plants grow on the dark floor of a dense rainforest. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: What is carrying capacity?
c: the weight an animal can carry
the largest population an ecosystem can support
the number of ecosystems on Earth
items.e: Food, water and space limit populations.

items.q: What is an ecosystem?
c: only the animals in a forest
all the living things in an area and the non-living things they interact with
items.e: Biotic and abiotic parts interact.

items.q: Why is only about 10% of energy passed on to the next level of a food chain?
c: Most energy is used for life processes or lost as heat.
items.e: This is shown in an energy pyramid.

items.q: Palesa needs an example of competition (organisms need the same limited resource). Which is the best example?
c: ants protect acacia trees and live in their thorns
trees grow taller to reach the same sunlight
a tapeworm lives in an animal's intestine
items.e: That is competition.

items.q: Daniel needs an example of mutualism (both benefit). Which is the best example?
c: fungi on plant roots get sugar and help roots take in water
trees grow taller to reach the same sunlight
moss grows on the bark of a tree
items.e: That is mutualism.

items.q: Corals die when sea water becomes too warm. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Seedlings grow towards a window. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Kgomotso observes that a frog eats a fly. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In predation, one organism hunts and eats another.

items.q: A bird nests in a tree and the tree is not affected. What kind of relationship is this?
items.e: One benefits; the other is not helped or harmed.

items.q: Ethan observes that lions and hyenas hunt the same zebras. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In competition, organisms need the same limited resource.

items.q: Bees get nectar and flowers get pollinated. What kind of relationship is this?
items.e: Both species gain.

items.q: Lungile observes that barnacles ride on a whale without hurting it. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In commensalism, one benefits and the other is not helped or harmed.

items.q: Jabu observes that a tapeworm lives in an animal's intestine. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed.

items.q: Which organisms recycle nutrients from dead matter back into the soil?
items.e: Fungi and bacteria are decomposers.

items.q: A tick feeds on a deer's blood. What kind of relationship is this?
items.e: The deer is harmed.

items.q: Ethan observes that lice live on a person's head. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed.

items.q: Cacti survive in deserts where it rarely rains. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Liam needs an example of competition (organisms need the same limited resource). Which is the best example?
c: weeds and corn take the same water
fungi on plant roots get sugar and help roots take in water
a hawk dives for a rabbit
barnacles ride on a whale without hurting it
items.e: That is competition.

items.q: Nadia observes that trees grow taller to reach the same sunlight. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In competition, organisms need the same limited resource.

items.q: Look at the ocean food web. A disease kills most of the seaweed. Which population would most likely go down first?
items.e: The sea urchin eats only seaweed. Without them, the sea urchin has little food.

items.q: Use the meadow food web. Most of the hawks are removed from the meadow. Which population would most likely go up at first?
items.e: Only the hawk eats snakes. With fewer predators, more snakes survive.

items.q: Food chain: phytoplankton → krill → whale. If all the krill were removed, what would most likely happen first?
c: There would probably be more phytoplankton.
There would probably be fewer phytoplankton.
items.e: With no krill eating them, more phytoplankton survive.

items.q: Food chain: seaweed → periwinkle → crab → herring gull. If all the crabs were removed, what would most likely happen first?
c: There would probably be fewer periwinkles.
There would probably be more periwinkles.
items.e: With no crabs eating them, more periwinkles survive.

items.q: Food chain: acorns → wood mouse → tawny owl. If the number of acorns fell, what would most likely happen to the wood mice?
c: There would be less food, so their numbers would fall.
items.e: Animals depend on what they eat.

items.q: Where does the energy in almost every food chain come from first?
items.e: Plants use the Sun's energy to make food.

items.q: This is a coral reef food web. Most of the small fish are removed from the coral reef. Which population would most likely go up at first?
items.e: Only the small fish eats zooplankton. With fewer predators, more zooplankton survive.

items.q: Look at the coral reef food web. A disease kills most of the seaweed. Which population would most likely go down first?
items.e: The green turtle eats only seaweed. Without them, the green turtle has little food.

items.q: A wolf eats deer. A deer eats grass. What is the deer?
items.e: Deer eat only plants.

items.q: This is a school garden food web. Most of the snakes are removed from the school garden. Which population would most likely go up at first?
items.e: Only the snake eats mynahs. With fewer predators, more mynahs survive.

items.q: Use the mangrove swamp food web. A disease kills most of the mudskippers. Which population would most likely go down first?
items.e: The heron eats only mudskippers. Without them, the heron has little food.

items.q: Snowshoe hares eat plants. Lynx eat hares. If the number of hares falls, what happens to the lynx?
c: Lynx start making their own food.
There is less food, so the number of lynx falls.
items.e: Predators depend on their prey.

items.q: Use the mangrove swamp food web. A disease kills most of the algae. Which population would most likely go down first?
items.e: The snail eats only algae. Without them, the snail has little food.

items.q: Food chain: seaweed → periwinkle → crab → herring gull. If the number of seaweed fell, what would most likely happen to the periwinkles?
c: There would be less food, so their numbers would fall.
items.e: Animals depend on what they eat.

items.q: Use the desert food web. A disease kills most of the desert grass. Which population would most likely go down first?
items.e: The beetle eats only desert grass. Without them, the beetle has little food.

items.q: Food chain: oak leaves → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk. If all the blue tits were removed, what would most likely happen first?
c: There would probably be more caterpillars.
There would probably be fewer caterpillars.
items.e: With no blue tits eating them, more caterpillars survive.

items.q: Food chain: dandelion → snail → song thrush → cat. If the number of snails fell, what would most likely happen to the song thrushes?
c: There would be less food, so their numbers would fall.
items.e: Animals depend on what they eat.

items.q: Food chain: phytoplankton → krill → whale. If the number of krill fell, what would most likely happen to the whales?
c: There would be less food, so their numbers would fall.
items.e: Animals depend on what they eat.

items.q: Look at the ocean food web. Most of the orcas are removed from the ocean. Which population would most likely go up at first?
items.e: Only the orca eats sea otters. With fewer predators, more sea otters survive.

items.q: Lake food chain: algae → zooplankton → minnow → walleye → osprey. What eats the walleye?
items.e: The arrow from walleye points to the osprey.
